channel.title: Thirsty Planet
channel.description: Understanding water, before it's gone. The hidden water inside everyday things, the water industry in plain words, and the places already solving it.

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Steel
item.description:
A tonne of steel takes about 28,000 litres of water through the works and keeps about 3,300 of them, by the industry's own survey. The rest goes back to the river, warmer and, at a well run plant, cleaner than it came. The world makes two billion tonnes a year, so the consumption comes to several cubic kilometres and the withdrawal to twenty times that.
Almost all of it is cooling. A blast furnace, a basic oxygen converter, a continuous caster and a hot rolling mill are each machines for handling metal at over a thousand degrees, and every one of them is cooled by water running through its walls, rolls and hearths. The rest quenches red hot coke and slag, scrubs the dust out of furnace gas, and descales the slab under the rolls. The water that is consumed is what evaporates from the cooling towers and the quench.
The industry is changing, and the water will change with it. Steel from scrap in an electric furnace uses a fraction of the water of steel from ore in a blast furnace, and steel from hydrogen and iron ore, which the industry is building to cut its carbon, will consume more water at the electrolysis than it saves at the coke ovens. It is a water story told in the shape of a furnace.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Power Stations
item.description:
The largest user of fresh water in the United States is power stations, ahead of farming. About 41 percent of all the fresh water withdrawn in the country goes to cooling them, according to the national survey, ahead of irrigation, and the same is true in much of Europe.
The reason is steam. A coal, gas or nuclear plant boils water to spin a turbine, and the steam has to be condensed back to water to be boiled again. Condensing it takes a river of cooling water: a large plant on a once through system draws a hundred thousand litres for every megawatt hour it makes and returns nearly all of it, warmer. A plant with cooling towers draws far less and evaporates most of what it draws, about 2,500 litres a megawatt hour, which is gone.
The number is moving. Wind and solar use almost no water, gas plants use less than coal, and in the summer of 2022 France turned down reactors because the Rhône was too warm to take their heat. The grid is becoming less thirsty by the year, and the reason has nothing to do with water policy: the thirsty plants are closing.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Leather and tanning
item.description:
Of all the industries in this series, tanning is the one whose water frightens treatment engineers most, and it is the oldest of them all.
A tannery turns a raw hide, which would rot in days, into leather, which lasts decades, through a chain of baths: salt soaked out, hair and flesh removed with lime and sulphide, the hide pickled in acid and tanned with chromium. Every bath goes to the drain, and what leaves carries salt, lime, sulphide, chromium and an organic load of hair, flesh and blood many times that of sewage. It is the textile effluent with metals and poison gas added.
The industry moved, over fifty years, from Europe to the countries with the hides and the labour, and the damage moved with it. Kanpur on the Ganges, Hazaribagh in Dhaka, Ranipet in Tamil Nadu, Fez in Morocco: rivers the colour of dye, chromium in the wells. In 2017 Bangladesh moved Dhaka's entire tanning district to a new estate with a common treatment plant. Whether the plant runs is the question I have gone to see.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Hydrogen
item.description:
Green hydrogen is made by running electricity through water. The chemistry is fixed: nine litres of water become one kilogram of hydrogen and eight kilograms of oxygen. In practice a plant uses two to three times that, for cooling and for purifying the water first, so a kilogram of hydrogen leaves the plant with twenty to thirty litres behind it.
That is a small number per kilogram and a large one per plant. The projects announced in Saudi Arabia, Oman, Namibia, Chile and Australia are sized in millions of tonnes a year, and a million tonnes of hydrogen means tens of millions of cubic metres of water, in places where the whole point is the desert sun. Nearly all of them will desalinate, which adds energy and a brine to the coast.
The water is manageable, and the industry knows it, and the plants are designed for it. What it does is make green hydrogen a coastal industry as much as a solar one, and it puts a new, very large water user next to the fishing towns and the desalination plants that were there first.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Data Centres
item.description:
Google's data centres consumed about 23 billion litres of water in 2023, by the company's own environmental report, up from about 21 billion the year before. Microsoft's use grew by a third in a single year. The reason is heat.
A rack of servers turns electricity into heat, all of it, and the heat has to go somewhere. The cheapest way to get rid of it is to evaporate water in a cooling tower, and the water that evaporates is gone from the river or the aquifer it came from. A large data centre can consume as much water as a town of tens of thousands of people, and the buildings are being put up in dry places, because dry places have cheap land and cheap power.
Artificial intelligence has made the numbers move. Training and running the large models takes far more computing per task than a search did, and one widely cited study put a chatbot's water at about half a litre for every twenty to fifty questions, once the cooling and the power station are counted. The industry is responding, with closed loop cooling and pledges to replenish more than it uses. Whether those pledges add up is the water question of the decade.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Copper
item.description:
A tonne of copper takes about seventy thousand litres of water to get out of the ground, at the average of the mines that publish their figures. The world uses about 26 million tonnes a year, and the transition to electric cars, wind turbines and grids will need something like twice that by the 2040s. About a quarter of it comes from Chile, and most of Chile's comes from the Atacama, the driest desert on Earth.
The water is in the mill. Copper ore is less than one percent metal, so a tonne of copper is a hundred tonnes of rock, crushed to powder and floated in tanks of water and chemicals where the copper minerals rise with the froth and the rock sinks. The wet waste goes to a tailings dam. For a century the mines of the Atacama drew that water from the aquifers under the salt flats, and the flats, the lagoons and the villages that shared them dried.
The industry has done what it had to. The largest mines now pump seawater up three thousand metres from the coast, desalinated or raw, and Chile's rules have forced the rest to follow. It is the clearest case in mining of a thirsty industry moving its water to the sea, and it was pushed there by a desert that ran out.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Concrete
item.description:
Concrete is the second most used substance on Earth. Only water is used more, and concrete is made of it. The world pours around thirty billion tonnes a year, and a study in 2018 put the water consumed in making it at about nine percent of global industrial water withdrawals, more than any other manufactured product.
The water is in three places. A cubic metre of concrete needs about 150 to 200 litres of water to mix, which reacts with the cement and stays in the slab. It needs several times that again to cure, sprayed or ponded on the surface for days so the cement hardens properly. And the aggregate, the sand and gravel that make up three quarters of the mix, is washed with water at the quarry, which is often the largest share of all.
What makes it a water story is where it happens. Concrete is poured where cities are growing, and the cities growing fastest are in India, the Gulf, Africa and dry parts of China, on the same aquifers the farms and the people draw on. A tower in a desert is built with local water, at a rate of about a swimming pool per floor.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Gold
item.description:
A gold ring weighs about five grams, and the mine that produced its gold used about 3,500 litres of water to do it, by the best global average published. Per kilogram of metal, gold is one of the thirstiest things on Earth: around 700,000 litres, because a tonne of ore yields a gram or two of gold and every tonne has to be crushed to flour and washed.
The washing is with cyanide. Gold dissolves in a weak cyanide solution, so the crushed rock is soaked in it, in tanks or in great heaps, the gold is pulled out of the liquid, and the wet, cyanide bearing rock, the tailings, is pumped to a dam. Tailings dams are among the largest structures humans build, and when one fails, as at Baia Mare in 2000 or Brumadinho in 2019, a river dies for a hundred kilometres.
The large mines have learned to recycle most of their water and to destroy the cyanide before it leaves. The small ones, the artisanal miners who produce a fifth of the world's gold, use mercury instead, in rivers, with their hands, and that is the worst water story in mining.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: An egg
item.description:
One egg carries about 196 litres of water, and the hen drank almost none of it.
A laying hen eats around 110 grams of feed a day, mostly maize and soybean meal, and lays an egg most days. Grow all that grain, divide its water by the eggs, and an egg comes to about 3,300 litres per kilo, or 196 litres for a 60 gram egg, by the Water Footprint Network's method. Her own drinking water is a few percent of that.
The number that makes the egg interesting is the one per gram of protein. Eggs need about 29 litres for a gram of protein, close to milk, a third of pork and a quarter of beef. Among animal foods, the egg is one of the most efficient there is, and about four fifths of its water is rain on a field of grain.
As always, the field decides the rest. Maize irrigated in a dry region and soy grown on rain in Brazil carry very different water, and the carton does not say which the hen ate.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Chicken
item.description:
A kilogram of chicken carries about 4,325 litres of water in the global averages, against roughly 6,000 for pork and 15,400 for beef. It is the least thirsty meat by a wide margin, and the reason is arithmetic.
A broiler chicken reaches its slaughter weight in about six weeks on around 1.6 kilograms of feed for every kilogram it gains. A pig needs closer to three, a cow six or more. The feed is where the water is, in the maize and soy that were grown, mostly on rain, to fill the bird's ration. Less feed per kilogram means less water per kilogram, and chicken wins that sum against every other animal.
Two things people miss. The first is that 4,300 litres is still four times the water in a kilogram of wheat, because feeding grain to an animal always loses most of it. The second is the plant. A chicken processing plant uses twenty to thirty litres of water per bird for scalding, washing and chilling, and its effluent is one of the strongest in the food industry.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Cheese
item.description:
It takes about ten litres of milk to make a kilogram of hard cheese, and a litre of milk carries about a thousand litres of water. So a kilo of cheese should carry ten thousand. The Water Footprint Network's figure is about 3,200, and the difference is the most interesting thing about the number.
When milk is made into cheese, nine tenths of it becomes whey, and whey is a product too: dried into protein powder, fed to pigs, digested for gas. The footprint method splits the milk's water between the cheese and the whey in proportion to their value, and the cheese carries only its share. The water was all used. It is divided differently.
The rest of the story is the cow, as with milk and beef: 96 percent of the water grew the feed, and whether it was rain on pasture or a river in a dry valley depends on the farm. And the cheese plant has a water story of its own, in the brine bath where the cheese is salted and in the cleaning of every pipe the milk touched.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Almonds
item.description:
A single almond takes about twelve litres of irrigation water to grow in California, where four out of five of the world's almonds come from. A kilogram of shelled almonds, in the global averages, runs to around 16,000 litres, most of it pumped.
The reason is geography. Almonds need a mild wet winter and a long hot dry summer, and the Central Valley has exactly that, which means every drop the trees drink between April and September comes from a canal or a well. The orchards more than doubled in twenty years, to well over a million acres, and a tree cannot be fallowed in a drought the way a field of tomatoes can. So in the dry years the wells ran, the valley floor sank, and the almond became the villain of California's water story.
It is a crop with a high value per drop and a low tolerance for a dry year. Both are true at once, and that is the story.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: ZLD
item.description:
There is a kind of factory that has no outfall. Nothing liquid leaves it. Every drop of water it uses is recovered and used again, and everything that was dissolved in that water comes out at the end as a solid, in bags. The industry calls it zero liquid discharge, ZLD, and it is the answer to the question every membrane plant leaves behind: what to do with the brine.
The process is a chain. Treatment, then membranes, which recover most of the water and leave a brine. Then evaporators, which boil the brine down using recovered heat, and finally a crystalliser, which turns the last of it into salt. The water is all recovered. The salt is dry. The energy bill is the catch, because boiling water is the most expensive thing that can be done to it.
In January 2011 the Madras High Court ordered every dyeing unit in Tirupur, the knitwear capital of southern India, to close until it achieved zero liquid discharge, and a whole industrial town learned to run these plants. It was expensive, and it is the clearest demonstration anywhere that the technology works when somebody insists.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Ultrapure water
item.description:
Most of this series is about making water clean enough to drink. There is an industry that needs water far cleaner than that, so clean that drinking it would be unpleasant and piping it through steel would dissolve the steel.
It is called ultrapure water, and it is what a semiconductor plant rinses its silicon wafers in, what a pharmaceutical plant makes injections from, and what a power station boils in its turbines. In a chip fab a single dissolved ion or a particle a few nanometres across on a wafer is a ruined circuit, so the water has to have, as nearly as physics allows, nothing in it. The measure is electrical: pure water barely conducts, and ultrapure water is pushed to 18.2 megohm centimetres, the theoretical limit, at which there is almost nothing dissolved to carry a charge.
It is made from ordinary tap water by a chain that starts with the reverse osmosis of the desalination article and goes far past it: two passes of membranes, an electric field to strip the last ions, ultraviolet light to break down organic molecules, resin polishers, and filters finer than anything in a drinking water plant. The water arrives at the wafer purer than anything in nature.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Reverse osmosis
item.description:
Reverse osmosis is the process behind nearly every drop of desalinated or recycled water on Earth, and its name describes exactly what it is: nature's process, run backwards, by force.
Put salty water and fresh water either side of a membrane that lets only water through, and the fresh water flows towards the salt. That is osmosis, the same pull that moves water into a plant's roots. For seawater the pull is worth about 27 bar. To make water go the other way, out of the salt and through the membrane, a plant has to push harder than that, and seawater plants run their pumps at 55 to 80 bar. The pumps are where the energy goes.
What comes through is water with about 99 percent of the salt removed. What stays behind is a brine, half the volume and twice the salt, and where that goes is the hardest question in the business.
Thirty years ago a seawater plant used around 8 kilowatt hours for every cubic metre. Today the best run at about 3. The membranes got better and, above all, the pressure in the brine is now recovered rather than thrown away. It is one of the quieter engineering successes of the age.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Phosphorus
item.description:
Nitrogen, the subject of the last article, can be sent back to the air, because that is where it came from. Phosphorus cannot. It came from rock, mined in a handful of countries, and once it has passed through a crop, a person and a sewer it is either in the sea or in the sludge at the back of the treatment plant.
Phosphorus in a lake grows algae, and in freshwater it is usually the nutrient that decides how much. Lake Erie turned green in the 1960s on phosphorus from detergents and sewage, and recovered when both were controlled. Sewage works now precipitate phosphorus out with iron or aluminium, or use bacteria that hoard it, and the limits have fallen to around a milligram per litre from the eight that arrives.
The interesting part is where it goes. The phosphate rock the world's fertiliser comes from is concentrated in Morocco above all, and it is finite. A city's sewage contains a large share of the phosphorus its food arrived with, and the plants that recover it as a crystal called struvite are, in a small way, mining their own sludge.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: pH
item.description:
Of all the numbers on a water report, pH is the one everyone half remembers from school and the one a plant operator checks first.
It measures how acid or alkaline water is, on a scale from 0 to 14 where 7 is neutral. The scale is logarithmic, so each step is ten times the last: water at pH 5 is ten times more acid than water at pH 6 and a hundred times more than at 7. Rain sits near 5.6, tap water between 6.5 and 8.5, seawater at about 8.1. A dye house's effluent leaves at 10 or 11, which is why the first thing an effluent plant does is neutralise it.
pH decides almost everything downstream. Fish sicken outside a narrow band. The bacteria that clean water in a treatment plant stop eating outside theirs. Coagulants only work in their window. And water that is slightly acid dissolves the pipes it flows through, which is how Flint, Michigan poisoned its children with lead in 2014: the city changed its water source and stopped adding the chemical that kept the pipes' lining intact.
One number, checked first, for good reason. The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: PFAS
item.description:
In 2024 the United States set its first national limit for two chemicals in drinking water at four nanograms per litre. Four parts per trillion. That is a single drop in twenty Olympic swimming pools, and it is the strictest drinking water limit ever set for anything.
The chemicals are PFOA and PFOS, the best known members of a family called PFAS, made since the 1940s for anything that needed to shed water or grease: non stick pans, waterproof jackets, food packaging, firefighting foam. The carbon fluorine bond that makes them useful makes them indestructible. They do not rot, burn or break down in sunlight. Every one made is still here, and they are in the blood of nearly every person tested.
They got into water from factories, from the foam used at airports and military bases, and from sewage sludge spread on fields. Getting them out is possible, with activated carbon, ion exchange resin or reverse osmosis, and it is expensive, and the industry that I work in has spent the last five years learning to do it. The chemicals themselves still have to go somewhere. That part is unsolved.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Nitrogen
item.description:
Every sewage works receives about 40 milligrams of nitrogen in every litre, nearly all of it as ammonia, nearly all of it from urine, and for most of the twentieth century it was let straight through to the river.
Nitrogen in a river does three kinds of harm. Ammonia is toxic to fish. Bacteria that eat ammonia consume oxygen doing it, so it suffocates a river the way organic matter does. And nitrogen is fertiliser, so downstream, in lakes and estuaries, it grows algae until the algae die, rot, and take the oxygen with them. The dead zones at the mouths of the Mississippi and in the Baltic are made of nitrogen.
Removing it takes two sets of bacteria that want opposite things. One set, given plenty of air, turns ammonia into nitrate. The other, starved of air, turns nitrate into nitrogen gas, which leaves the water and returns to the atmosphere it came from. A modern plant runs both, in tanks side by side, and the gas that bubbles off is the same nitrogen that a fertiliser factory took from the air in the first place.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Membranes
item.description:
The most important piece of equipment in modern water treatment is a sheet of plastic with holes in it too small to imagine.
A membrane is a filter taken to its limit. Sand catches grit. Cloth catches lint. A microfiltration membrane, with pores a tenth of a micron across, catches bacteria. Ultrafiltration, at a hundredth of a micron, catches viruses. Nanofiltration begins to catch dissolved molecules. Reverse osmosis, at the bottom of the scale, holds back salt and lets almost nothing but water through.
Each step down the scale costs more pressure, because pushing water through smaller holes is harder work, and each step catches something the last one could not. A modern reuse plant, in Singapore or in a textile mill in India, is that scale laid out in a row: biology first, then membranes in order of fineness, until what comes out is cleaner than what the city drinks.
The membrane is why water can now be recycled at all. The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Leaks
item.description:
The world's water utilities lose about 126 billion cubic metres a year from their own pipes, a third of everything they treat and pump. It is called non revenue water, it leaks from mains that are often a century old, and it is worth about 40 billion dollars a year in water that was cleaned, pressurised and then poured into the ground.
The losses are uneven. A well run utility in the Netherlands or Denmark loses under a tenth. London loses about a quarter. Cities in South Asia, Africa and Latin America routinely lose half, and some of that water is not leaking but being taken, through illegal connections and meters that do not turn.
What makes it a story is that it is the cheapest water there is. Every cubic metre saved from a leak is a cubic metre that was already treated and delivered, needing no new dam, no new plant, no new well. The utilities that have gone after it, Tokyo above all, have found more water in their pipes than in any new source, and I have yet to see a city that could not.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Hard water
item.description:
The scale in a kettle, the white film on a shower screen and the reason soap will not lather in some towns are all the same two minerals: calcium and magnesium. Together they are what the water industry calls hardness.
Hardness is the part of a water's dissolved solids that came from limestone and chalk. Rain soaks through the rock, dissolves a little of it, and arrives at the tap carrying it. Heat the water and the calcium comes back out as limescale. That is the whole mechanism, and it is the most harmless complaint water can have. The World Health Organization sets no health limit for it, and hard water contributes calcium and magnesium to the diet.
For industry it is a different matter. Scale in a boiler insulates the metal from the water and wastes fuel; scale on a membrane blocks it. So plants soften their water, swapping calcium for sodium on a resin that is reset with salt, or dose chemicals that hold the scale in solution. The kettle, the boiler and the reverse osmosis plant are all fighting the same two minerals.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Greywater
item.description:
Half to two thirds of the water that leaves a home was only lightly used. It ran through the shower, the basin and the washing machine, and it carries soap, skin, lint and warmth, and very little else. The industry calls it greywater, and it is the easiest water in the house to use twice.
The obvious second use is the toilet, which takes about a quarter of a home's water and does not need drinking water to do its job. A greywater system catches the shower and laundry water, filters and disinfects it, stores it briefly, and pumps it to the cisterns. Australia's cities fitted tens of thousands of them in the long drought of the 2000s. Jordan and Cyprus require them in new buildings.
Why is it not everywhere? Because mains water is cheap, the plumbing is expensive to retrofit, and greywater goes off within a day if it is stored untreated. It pays in new buildings, in dry countries and in homes with gardens. It rarely pays as an afterthought.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Disinfection
item.description:
The step in water treatment that has saved more lives than any medicine is a small dose of chlorine added to water that already looks clean.
Disinfection is the last stage before water goes to a city, and its job is to kill what the filters could not: bacteria, viruses and parasites too small to see. Three tools do it. Chlorine, since 1908, cheap and effective, and the only one that keeps working in the pipes. Ultraviolet light, which breaks the DNA of anything that passes the lamp and leaves no taste. Ozone, a gas made from air on site, the strongest of the three and the most expensive.
Each has a weakness. Chlorine forms byproducts and cannot kill the parasite Cryptosporidium, which made 400,000 people ill in Milwaukee in 1993. UV and ozone leave no residual, so the water is unprotected the moment it leaves the plant. Most cities use two of the three, and the chlorine smell at the tap is the residual, doing its job on the way to you.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Desalination
item.description:
About one percent of the world's people drink the sea. In the Gulf it is most of them, and in Israel it is the majority of what comes out of the tap.
Desalination is the removal of salt from seawater, and for most of its history it meant boiling. The plants of the Gulf flashed seawater into steam in a chain of vessels and condensed it, using the waste heat of the power stations beside them. It worked, and it used enormous energy. Since the 1990s the industry has moved to reverse osmosis, pushing seawater through membranes at fifty to eighty times atmospheric pressure, and the energy per cubic metre has fallen by more than half.
The world now makes about 100 million cubic metres of desalinated water a day, from more than twenty thousand plants. The cost has fallen below a dollar a cubic metre, which is expensive water for farming and cheap water for a city that has no other. The catch is the brine, half the intake at twice the salt, returned to the sea, and the electricity, which decides whether a plant is a solution or a coal fired one.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Day Zero
item.description:
Day Zero is a term the water industry did not have until 2018, when Cape Town gave it one. It means the day a city's dams fall to the level at which the taps are switched off and water is handed out at collection points instead.
It is worth being precise about what it is. Day Zero is a projection, not an event. It is the date, calculated every week from the dam levels, the rate of consumption and the expected rain, on which the reservoirs would reach the point where the pumps can no longer draw. A city that reduces its consumption pushes the date back. A city that gets rain pushes it back further. Cape Town did both, and the date, once set for April 2018, moved into May, then June, then was quietly withdrawn when the winter rains came.
The number that saved the city was the ration rather than the date: 50 litres per person per day, which cut consumption by more than half. That is a shower, a flush or two, cooking and drinking, and nothing else.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Coagulation
item.description:
One of the first things a water treatment plant does to a river is add aluminium to it. On purpose, by the tonne. It is the oldest chemical trick in the business, and it is called coagulation.
River water is cloudy with particles too small to settle and too small for a sand filter to catch: clay, algae, colour from peat, the fragments of everything upstream. They stay suspended because each one carries a small negative charge, and they repel one another. Add a salt of aluminium or iron and the charge is cancelled. The particles touch, stick, and clump into flocs the size of snowflakes, which sink in a tank or are caught by a filter. Clear water is what is left.
The dose is set by a row of six beakers on a laboratory bench, stirred together with a ladder of doses, and read by eye. A plant serving a million people is run, in the end, on the jar that cleared best.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: CETP
item.description:
A dye house in Tirupur is a shed with a few machines, run by a family, and it cannot afford a treatment plant. Neither can the two hundred sheds around it. Together, they can. That is the idea behind a common effluent treatment plant, a CETP, and India has built hundreds of them.
The logic is simple: one plant, at the bottom of the cluster, fed by a network of drains from every factory, built to treat the mixed effluent of all of them, and paid for by the factories in proportion to what they send. The plant gets the scale it needs, and the small factories get a kidney they could never build alone.
The difficulties are the ones a shared thing always has. The plant receives whatever anyone sends, and one factory's spill upsets the biology for everyone. Every member would rather someone else paid. And the plant belongs to nobody, which means, in a bad year, it is run by nobody. Whether a CETP works is decided less by its engineering than by its governance, and I have seen both kinds.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Brine
item.description:
Every membrane plant produces two streams. One is the clean water everyone came for. The other carries everything the clean water left behind, and the industry calls it brine.
A seawater desalination plant sends about half its intake back to the sea as brine, at twice the sea's salt. Inland, where there is no sea, the brine from a reuse plant or a brackish well has nowhere obvious to go, and that is where the real engineering and the real cost of water recovery now sit. Discharge it and the river gets the salt. Evaporate it and the energy bill climbs. Recover the salt from it, which is where the interesting work is, and you have built a small chemical plant beside your water plant.
Globally, desalination produces about one and a half litres of brine for every litre of fresh water. The membrane solved the water. It handed the salt to someone else, and this is who.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Plain Water: BOD
item.description:
The water industry has two numbers for how dirty water is, and the second one is measured by sealing a bottle in the dark for five days.
It is called BOD, biochemical oxygen demand. A sample is seeded with bacteria, sealed in a bottle at 20 degrees with no light, and left. After five days the oxygen in the bottle is measured again, and the difference is the BOD: the oxygen that bacteria actually used, eating what they could actually eat, in the time a river might give them.
Its sibling, COD, does the same job with strong chemicals in two hours and counts everything. The ratio between the two is one of the most useful things an engineer can know about a water. Sewage has a BOD about half its COD, because most of what is in it is food. A textile effluent might be a fifth or a tenth, because much of its load is dye that bacteria cannot touch. That ratio says, before a plant is designed, whether biology alone can clean the water.
The five days, by the way, is the time water took to reach the sea in England in 1908. The industry kept the number.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Arsenic
item.description:
Bangladesh has the largest mass poisoning in history, and it was caused by a public health success.
In the 1970s and 1980s, aid agencies and the government sank millions of hand pumped tube wells across the country, to replace the pond and river water that spread cholera and killed children by the hundred thousand. The wells worked. Child mortality fell. Nobody tested the water for arsenic, because nobody thought to, and the sediments of the Ganges delta, laid down from the Himalayas over thousands of years, release arsenic into the groundwater at levels far above anything safe.
The poisoning is slow. Skin lesions appear after years, then cancers of the skin, lung and bladder after decades. Around twenty million people in Bangladesh still drink water above the country's own limit, and the WHO guideline is five times stricter than that. I have spent time in Bangladesh, and the painted wells, red for unsafe and green for safe, are the most sobering piece of water infrastructure I know.
Filters work, deeper wells work, and rain and treated surface water work. What has been slow is the money and the attention.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Plain Water: Antiscalants
item.description:
Every reverse osmosis plant has a small tank of chemical beside the pumps, dosed at a few milligrams per litre, without which the plant would stop within days. It is called an antiscalant, and it is the least known critical chemical in the water business.
The problem it solves is the kettle's problem, at pressure. A membrane concentrates everything it rejects, and on the brine side of the membrane the calcium, sulphate and bicarbonate that were comfortably dissolved in the feed are pushed several times past the point at which they would come out of solution. They crystallise, on the membrane surface, as scale, and scale blocks the membrane the way it furs a kettle element.
An antiscalant is a molecule, usually a phosphonate or a polymer, that sits on the surface of a forming crystal and stops it growing. It does not remove the hardness. It persuades the hardness to stay dissolved a little longer than chemistry says it should, long enough to leave with the brine.
Get the dose right and the membranes last seven years. Get it wrong and they last a season. The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Myth: Water Can't Run Out
item.description:
The water cycle is true. The amount of water on Earth is fixed, it has been the same for billions of years, and every drop that evaporates comes down again somewhere. From that, most people conclude that water cannot run out, and it is the most comforting mistake in the subject.
Water itself never runs out. Fresh water does: fresh water in a particular place, at a particular time, clean enough to use. The rain over the ocean is no use to a farm. The rain in a monsoon week is no use in the dry season unless something stored it. And the water under the ground, which is what half the world's irrigation now pumps, is in many places older than farming, laid down in wetter ages thousands of years ago, and refilled at a rate that has nothing to do with how fast it is being spent. The Ogallala under the American plains, the aquifers of north west India, the Nubian sandstone under the Sahara: these are being mined, and the satellites that weigh the Earth's water can watch them fall.
The cycle is real. The bank account is local, and some of the accounts are being emptied.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Myth: Rain Is Pure Water
item.description:
Rain is the purest water most people will ever see. It has been evaporated by the sun, which leaves every salt and mineral behind, and it comes down with about ten milligrams of dissolved solids in a litre, against a few hundred in tap water. That is the true half of the myth.
The other half is what rain meets on the way down and where it lands. Every drop forms on a speck of dust, it washes the air of soot, pollen, sulphur and, we now know, PFAS, at levels that exceed the new drinking water limits nearly everywhere on Earth. Then it hits a roof, with its bird droppings, its moss, its lead flashing and its zinc, and runs into a gutter and a barrel, where the last of the story is written by whatever grows in the dark.
Rain is excellent water to harvest, and Chennai, Bermuda and half of rural Australia run on it. It is water to be filtered and disinfected like any other, and the sense in which it is pure is the sense that matters least to a stomach.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Myth: Flushable wipes are flushable
item.description:
"Flushable wipes are flushable." The packet says so, the wipe goes down, and the sewer disagrees.
A flush proves nothing. Almost anything small enough will leave a toilet bowl. The question is what happens in the pipe, and the answer for most wet wipes is that nothing happens. Toilet paper is made to fall apart in water within seconds. A wipe is a nonwoven fabric, often bonded with plastic fibres, made to stay in one piece while wet, which is its whole purpose and its whole problem.
In the sewer, wipes snag, collect, and bind with the cooking fat that also should not be there, into masses that block pipes and pumps. The largest of these, found under Whitechapel in London in 2017, weighed 130 tonnes and stretched 250 metres. Britain's water companies clear around 300,000 sewer blockages a year and say most are wipes and fat.
The industry's verdict is plain: toilets are for the two things the body produces and paper. Everything else goes in the bin, whatever the packet says.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Myth: Boiling water removes everything
item.description:
"If in doubt, boil it." Good advice, and it covers half of what can be wrong with water.
Boiling kills. One minute at a rolling boil, three at altitude, and every bacterium, virus and parasite in the water is dead, including the Cryptosporidium that chlorine cannot touch. That is why a boil water notice is the right response to a burst main or a failed filter, and why boiling has saved more lives than any other water treatment in history.
Boiling does not remove anything. Salt, nitrate, lead, arsenic, pesticides, the fluoride in the tap and the dissolved solids that make the kettle fur: all of it stays in the pan, and since some of the water leaves as steam, what remains is slightly more concentrated than before. The scale in the kettle is the proof. It is the dissolved minerals, made visible by the heat, and none of them went anywhere.
Two problems, two tools. Microbes: boil. Chemistry: a filter, a membrane, or a different source. The kettle only ever solved the first.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Myth: A bath uses more water than a shower
item.description:
"A shower uses less water than a bath." It depends, and the modern shower has quietly overturned the rule.
A full standard bath holds about 80 litres, and a large one 150. A typical shower head delivers 8 to 10 litres a minute, so a five minute shower is 40 to 50 litres and a bath wins by nothing. A power shower delivers 15 litres a minute or more, and ten minutes under one is 150 litres, a large bath. The average shower in Britain lasts seven to eight minutes, which puts it, at a typical head, level with a bath.
The line is easy to find. Time the shower, put a bucket under the head for a minute to measure the flow, and multiply. Under 80 litres and the shower wins. Over it and the bath was the economical choice all along.
The water is the smaller half of it. Heating that water is the largest energy use in most homes after the heating itself, and every litre of hot water, bath or shower, was heated by gas or electricity.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Wine
item.description:
Almost every farmer on Earth is trying to get more water to their crop. Winemakers are the strange exception. They spend their careers trying to make the plant a little thirsty.
A vine with plenty of water grows big, watery grapes and lots of leaves. A vine that has to work sends its roots down and produces small grapes with concentrated flavour, which is what ends up tasting like something. Growers call the technique deficit irrigation, and in parts of Europe the rules go further: several famous appellations simply forbid irrigation, on the grounds that a vineyard that needs watering is planted in the wrong place.
All of which makes the number a little awkward. A glass of wine still carries about 109 litres of water, and per litre wine costs roughly three times what beer does. Grapes are not especially thirsty; there just are not many of them per bottle, and the vine drinks rain all season either way.
The part worth watching is what heat is doing to those old rules. Regions that built their identity on never irrigating are facing summers their vines were not planted for, and some of the bans have quietly started to bend.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Avocado
item.description:
This series has spent a lot of posts arguing that a big water number is not automatically bad news. Chocolate drinks tropical rain. Coffee mostly does too. The avocado is where that argument stops.
The difference is where the water comes from. Cocoa trees stand in some of the wettest places on Earth and drink what falls on them. Avocados prefer dry Mediterranean climates, which means Chile, Spain, Mexico, California, and in those places the water arrives through a pipe. Someone pumped it out of a river or a well, and it was not available for anything else afterwards.
Petorca in Chile is the case everyone in the water world knows. A fruit growing province where plantations expanded fast, rivers ran low, and residents ended up receiving drinking water by tanker truck while orchards nearby stayed green. That is a truck in a village rather than a footprint calculation.
None of which makes avocados forbidden. It makes them the fruit where origin actually matters, and the sticker on the skin says more about water than any number on a chart.
The long version, with the fruit table and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: TDS
item.description:
Pick up a bottle of mineral water and look near the bottom of the label. There will be a line saying dry residue at 180 degrees, followed by a number. That number is TDS, total dissolved solids, and once you know it you will read water differently.
It is everything dissolved into the water: salt, calcium, magnesium, whatever the water met on its way through the ground. Rain has almost none. Tap water runs a few hundred milligrams per litre. Seawater sits around 35,000.
Two things follow. The first is that TDS is what water tastes like. Water with nothing in it tastes flat, which is why distilled water is unpleasant and why mineral water brands advertise their minerals instead of hiding them. The second is that dissolved is the hard problem in my industry. A filter catches things by being too small to let them through, and dissolved salt has come apart into pieces far smaller than any pore. You cannot strain it, settle it, or feed it to bacteria. The only ways out are a membrane at very high pressure, boiling, or a resin, and all three cost energy. That is why salt is the wall every water recycling project eventually hits.
The long version, with the scale, the measurement and the three ways out, is on the site.
